articles.title_orig: ‘Sending a message’: Nvidia signals more cautious stance on China after Huang’s departure
articles.title_zh: ‘Sending a message’: Nvidia signals more cautious stance on China after Huang’s departure
articles.content_orig:
In the wake of Jensen Huang's meteoric fall from grace at Nvidia, the embattled company appears to be growing more cautious about China as new export controls and increasingly fractious state politics further complicate the AI footrace between Washington and Beijing.
Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday that while Nvidia booked $2.4 billion in revenue from sales of the company's "Hopper" chips to China in its fiscal third quarter, the company has halted shipments of those chips to Chinese firms and is modeling no revenue from those sales going forward.
The announcement marks a major shift for the company, which under Huang's leadership had aggressively pursued license from the Trump administration to sell its products into the world's second-largest economy.
The Commerce Department initially implemented sweeping restrictions on Nvidia's ability to sell its advanced semiconductors in China in 2022 under the Biden administration, largely closing the Chinese market to Huang's company. The Trump administration loosened those restrictions in 2025 amid US-China trade talks, approving Nvidia to export H200 chips — now three generations behind the company's leading products — to China.
Sales of those chips to China have accounted for only a small fraction of Nvidia's data center revenue, comprising less than 1% of data center sales in its fiscal second quarter and roughly 2.2% in its fiscal third quarter. That's partially due to Beijing slow-walking import approvals of the chips as Xi Jinping pushes for Chinese firms to build on domestic hardware, reducing their dependence on the American market.
Yet Huang himself has for years insisted that the US should further open Nvidia's access to China, arguing that by restricting Chinese access to American chips and foregoing potential Chinese dependence on US technology, Washington is only encouraging China to accelerate its own technological progress.
"Local companies are very talented, and the export controls gave them the spirit and energy to accelerate their development," Huang said in 2025 at a conference in Taipei , per local reporting. He repeated the sentiment in October 2026, telling Bloomberg , "I think we [the US] made a mistake, and this mistake is hard to unwind."
Public reporting and government investigations have revealed a shadow trade for the company's most advanced chips that has developed despite the US export regime. Accounts on Douyin, the nation's version of TikTok, openly offer sanctioned chips such as Nvidia's Blackwell B300 to buyers in videos reviewed by Yahoo Finance.
Those sales, if they occur, would likely contravene US export controls. Congressional leaders have called for investigations into Nvidia's dealings with China, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has questioned whether Nvidia may have knowingly pressed forward with illicit sales to China.
"What was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said on Fox News . "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel."
Nvidia has said in multiple quarterly reports that it projects no compute revenue from China in forward-looking estimates, stating in its fiscal second quarter report, "Under the current rules and geopolitical landscape, we are unable to create and deliver a competitive product for wide distribution in China's data center market with the approval from both the USG and the Chinese government."
The company also announced on Tuesday that it had formed a new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, responsible for "board-level oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management." The board is set to be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, with directors Stephen Neal and John Dabiri also sitting as members.
Concerns over China's technological progress were exacerbated over the past year as details of Huang's affair with a Chinese national, whom the US intelligence service believes to be a Chinese asset, were brought to light.
The woman at the center of those allegations, Alice Huang, at one point led a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which has been tied to large quantities of imports of advanced Nvidia chips, prompting worries within the US Commerce Department that the company or its subsidiaries may have been funneling the technology into China, circumventing US export controls.
In cutting off Hopper sales to China as Kress announced Tuesday, Nvidia may be looking to get ahead of Washington, where several pieces of legislation look to severely curb exports of American silicon to China, further closing off Nvidia's access to Chinese buyers.
"They are not banned from shipping [H200s], but I think they're sending a message that they're trying to be good actors in this," KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst John Vinh said on Yahoo Finance's "The 8:30."
The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security on Tuesday introduced a new export rule designed to shutter third-party access to the computing capacity of US chips located in countries such as Singapore or Malaysia, requiring physical examinations of delivery sites and new licenses for companies looking to import large volumes of chips.
The rule comes after concerns in Washington that Nvidia chips have been sent to data centers in places like Singapore, where their computing power is rented to companies in China, exploiting a loophole in US export control policy.
Nvidia broke out Singapore in its revenue projections through the second quarter of 2025, at which time sales to the Southeast Asian city-state accounted for 22% of Nvidia's total revenue, up from 8% two years earlier. In the following quarter, Nvidia moved its revenue reporting to a model "based upon the location of the customers' headquarters," as opposed to "customer billing location."
To be sure, further restrictions from Washington on a market already largely closed to the chip designer aren't likely to impact sales, as Kress noted Tuesday that even with the Commerce Department's new export controls, "with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong."
Even so, there remain questions around why Nvidia pursued the Chinese market — and companies like Megaspeed — so aggressively under Jensen Huang's leadership, Chris McGuire, the former deputy senior director for technology and national security at the National Security Council, said on Tuesday. McGuire, who served in former President Joe Biden's administration between 2022 and 2024, was responsible for coordinating government policies related to US cooperation with China, per the Council on Foreign Relations, where he is now a senior fellow.
"U.S. export controls have still not caused Nvidia to lose a single sale — it sells every single chip it makes, and every chip that was sold to Chinese firms, Megaspeed, or any other shell company could have been sold to Microsoft, Amazon, SpaceX, Meta, Google, or to allied companies," McGuire said. "So the fact that these chips went to China or Megaspeed both helped Chinese companies and hurt American companies."
Huang, who resigned after disclosing multiple extramarital affairs, is now set to face questions in Washington about his company's approach to AI, as he and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have been scheduled to testify in closed-door briefings before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence ​Committee in early December.
Jeffrey Kessler, undersecretary for industry and security at Commerce Department, who reports to Secretary Howard Lutnick, is also slated to appear before Congress in December, where he is expected to face questions about reports that he potentially interfered with an ongoing investigation at the Commerce Department into Alice Huang's company Megaspeed.

articles.title_orig: Dow slides 600 points, Nasdaq seesaws as Nvidia earnings bounce fizzles: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow slides 600 points, Nasdaq seesaws as Nvidia earnings bounce fizzles: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares sank around 2% Wednesday after the company issued its first earnings report since the departure of former CEO Jensen Huang .
Trading in the neocloud companies was volatile, as CoreWeave sank about 3%, Iren fell about 2% and Nebius whipsawed.
Nvidia's third-quarter revenue came in at $115.84 billion, more than $6 billion above analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion topped the $125.1 billion consensus, according to LSEG.
The semiconductor giant continues to navigate the fallout from Huang's resignation last week. Shortly before the results, Huang made his first public statement since resigning last week, saying that he was open to returning to the company, after an outpouring of support from prominent tech figures .
But Harvey Jones, the new and first-ever chair of Nvidia's board, said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO.
″[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," interim CEO Colette Kress told Jim Cramer on CNBC's "Mad Money."
"This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers — that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breath of different customers."
The U.S. Commerce Department announced a legal change on Monday to try and stem China's access to the most advanced Nvidia chips — which are already under export controls effectively preventing their import into the country — by restricting Chinese companies' ability to access compute remotely in overseas data centers.
In a letter Wednesday, the House Energy and Commerce Committee asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear to discuss chip export controls, and requested a briefing from interim CEO Colette Kress by Dec. 2.
Nvidia told investors in its earnings commentary that it was "not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook," in keeping with its recent language on the country.
Huang is slated to appear before several Congressional committees in the coming weeks.
Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Tuesday, Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Huang and Lutnick have agreed to appear before the committee in December. It's slated to be Huang's second appearance on Capitol Hill in December, after the former Nvidia CEO reached an agreement with three House committees to appear for closed-door interviews on Dec. 1.
— CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO live: Company set to price stock between $70 and $78, as trading starts Thursday
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO live: Company set to price stock between $70 and $78, as trading starts Thursday
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is considering upsizing its initial public offering, people familiar with the details told CNBC, as the artificial intelligence lab weighs setting the price well above $80.
The company closed its order books and locked in total demand on Tuesday, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing. Institutional demand for the offering is around $400 billion, while retail demand is approaching $100 billion, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The orders are indications of interest and are not binding. All of the details are subject to change, and Anthropic will make final decisions Wednesday afternoon, the people said. Anthropic is expected to set its final IPO price after market close Wednesday.
Demand for the offering is higher than it was for Elon Musk's SpaceX , even though the rocket maker had a bigger market offering. SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq in June in by far the biggest IPO on record, ultimately raising $85.7 billion.
The AI lab said last week that it would offer 825 million shares in the IPO at a price range of between $70 and $78 per share, which would net up to $64.35 billion at the high end of that range.
A representative for Anthropic declined to comment.
Anthropic's listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds.
Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft , Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion in the IPO. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD.
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time."
Amodei co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027.
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said, it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.
The company has faced plenty of challenges during its meteoric rise over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO.
"Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort."

articles.title_orig: Trump expected to raise cases of Americans detained in China in meeting with Xi, families say
articles.title_zh: Trump expected to raise cases of Americans detained in China in meeting with Xi, families say
articles.content_orig:
President Trump is expected to again press Chinese President Xi Jinping to release two Americans wrongfully detained in China when the leaders meet , their families say, as Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.
Mr. Trump previously raised the detention of American scholar Youlin Chen with Xi during a meeting in Beijing in May, and confirmed discussing detained Americans with the Chinese leader again during his September visit to Washington. The leaders' upcoming bilateral meeting would mark the third time Mr. Trump has raised Chen's case and the second time he is expected to raise that of Min Zin, another American scholar who was detained in June.
Mr. Trump arrived in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, or APEC. He is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday, ahead of a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The families of the detained Americans say they have been assured Mr. Trump intends to raise the cases, though it remains unclear whether the issue will ultimately figure in his discussions with Xi, which are expected to cover a range of trade and national security matters.
Asked whether the president would raise the cases with Xi, the White House pointed to remarks he made earlier this month, when he said he discussed detained Americans with Xi "a lot" and cited the administration's record of freeing Americans. The State Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Sylvia Zin, whose husband Min Zin has been detained for nearly six months, said he is being held in solitary confinement at an undisclosed location, without access to legal counsel. She said the family recently learned he had been hospitalized last month for severe dehydration following a stomach illness and that the facility where he is being held has no heat.
"My worry for my husband's health and wellbeing increases with each passing day," she said.
"I am grateful for the President's commitment in continuing to raise my husband's wrongful detention, yet again," Sylvia Zin said. "My daughter and I remain hopeful in the President's ability to bring him home to us in time for the holidays."
The other American, Youlin Chen , has been detained in China since November 2024. He faces espionage charges stemming from U.S. government-funded research on detecting North Korean nuclear tests. His family denies the allegations, noting that his work relied on publicly available data and was conducted in collaboration with Chinese scientists.
His wife, Yufang Rong, said she has also received assurances that Mr. Trump intends to raise his case directly with Xi.
"I've been assured that President Trump remains firmly committed to securing Youlin's freedom and that he intends to raise Youlin's case with President Xi at both the APEC meeting and, if needed, the G20," she told CBS News.
The next G20 summit is scheduled for December at the president's golf resort in Doral, Florida. Xi is expected to attend, although Beijing has not confirmed his participation.
Min Zin is a naturalized American citizen who fled his native Myanmar during the pro-democracy movement of the 1980s. He was detained by Chinese authorities on June 3 after traveling from Thailand to the Chinese city of Kunming for an academic conference at the invitation of a Chinese professor. He runs a think tank that studies China's role in neighboring Myanmar, and his organization previously received U.S. government funding — which may have been a factor in attracting the scrutiny of Chinese intelligence authorities, U.S. officials have said.
Sylvia Zin previously told CBS News she believes he was lured to China and arrested on false charges. The State Department formally designated him as wrongfully detained in August.
Min Zin is being held by China's Ministry of State Security under a system known as Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location, or RSDL, which human rights groups describe as a form of secret detention. U.S. consular officials have been permitted brief, closely monitored monthly visits with him at a nearby hotel, according to his wife, but his family has not been allowed to see or speak directly with him.
Chinese authorities have accused Min Zin of activities endangering national security, including suspected espionage, allegations his family vehemently denies. Beijing has rejected the U.S. government's wrongful detention designation, maintaining that its authorities are acting in accordance with Chinese law.
The administration has repeatedly touted its record of bringing detained Americans home, including teacher Marc Fogel and ballet dancer Ksenia Karelina from Russia, and academic Dennis Coyle from Afghanistan. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said more than 100 detained Americans have been freed during Mr. Trump's second term.
Most recently, Mr. Trump said he personally appealed to Putin to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, the last American formally designated as wrongfully detained in Russia, who was freed in October without a prisoner swap. There are roughly 20 Americans imprisoned in Russia, and some of them are under review for potential designation by Rubio as wrongfully detained. Mr. Trump and Putin are also expected to meet one-on-one in China on Thursday.
But despite the president's personal interventions, neither of the two Americans held in China has been released.
Their cases have prompted scrutiny of the risks facing Americans traveling to China. In October, the State Department reinstated a "D" risk indicator on its China travel advisory, warning that Americans face a serious risk of wrongful detention there. The designation, also applied to six other countries including Russia, North Korea, Iran and Afghanistan, had been removed from China's advisory in November 2024 following a prisoner exchange. China's overall travel advisory remains at Level 2, with the State Department advising Americans to exercise increased caution.
Eric Lebson of Global Reach, an advocate for the detained Americans, said the administration is considering raising China's overall advisory to Level 3, which would advise Americans to reconsider travel. Such a move would be separate from the wrongful detention designation and could significantly affect academic exchanges, business travel and international conferences in China, Lebson said.
"It is uncharacteristic of the Chinese government to not engage on resolving matters of this type after two discussions about them at the presidential level," Lebson said, suggesting there may be disagreements within the Chinese government over how to handle the cases.
The potential push to secure the Americans' release comes as senior Trump administration officials have publicly disagreed over how aggressively to confront Beijing. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, have pressed for tighter restrictions on China's access to advanced American technology, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has resisted some of those measures, warning they could jeopardize relations with Beijing.
The disagreement has centered on efforts to prevent sensitive Nvidia chips from reaching China through third countries. Bessent publicly criticized the Commerce Department for delaying restrictions, while Mr. Trump defended Lutnick on Monday, saying he understood the concern that tougher measures could provoke a confrontation with Beijing. The president has at times favored a more accommodating approach to China, even as he has reportedly authorized tighter export controls.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Gulf states and tankers under fire as U.S. and Iran ramp back up tit-for-tat strikes
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Gulf states and tankers under fire as U.S. and Iran ramp back up tit-for-tat strikes
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is warning Americans in Bahrain to be extra careful after at least four attempted strikes by Iran in the last week.
"Americans in Bahrain should exercise heightened vigilance due to the increased threat of armed attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis and Iranian efforts to target U.S. government officials and facilities in the region," the U.S. Embassy said in a new security alert issued Wednesday. "Be aware of potential alerts, flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."
All of the launches were intercepted before causing any harm, according to U.S. Central Command. Iran was reportedly targeting U.S. radar sites in Bahrain. The latest round on Wednesday included attacks directed at Kuwait as well.
CENTCOM put out a statement on Wednesday afternoon saying no American military personnel have been injured in any of the strikes launched this week in a rebuttal to apparent rumors spreading online, it said.
The U.S. Treasury has targeted funding for the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in its latest round of sanctions tied to Operation Economic Outcast.
One of the targets of the sanctions was the Wa Ta'awanu Association, which the U.S. said is a charity that "provides cover for Hizballah's activities under the guise of delivering humanitarian services."
"The Iranian regime's attempts to infringe on Lebanon's sovereignty through terror proxies like Hizballah will not be tolerated," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "The U.S. government will continue to disrupt Iran's attempts to exert influence in the region and fund its proxies."
The sanctions also targeted an alleged gold and cash smuggling network run by Hezbollah and the IRGC's Quds Force.
The Hezbollah militant group has been fighting Israel in southern Lebanon for years, but the latest round of violence was sparked in the wake of the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. In solidarity, Hezbollah began targeting northern Israel with missile and drone launches, prompting an invasion by Israel.
The chief of Israel's military, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, met with U.S. Central Command leader Adm. Brad Cooper in Tel Aviv on Wednesday to discuss the current situation in the Middle East.
"During the meeting, the participants discussed regional developments and shared security challenges," Israeli officials said in a statement. "They also addressed the importance of deepening strategic and operational cooperation between the two militaries, strengthening coordination, and enhancing joint readiness to address a range of scenarios."
CENTCOM oversees military action in the Middle East and Cooper has become an important member of the Trump administration's Defense Department.
In addition, Zamir, Cooper and Mossad Director Roman Gofman took part in a trilateral meeting. Mossad is Israel's foreign intelligence agency, similar to the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency.
The U.S. and Israel have been debating whether to restart larger military action against Iran in the past several weeks after talks prior to Election Day fell apart. The U.S. launched a strike on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, which was categorized as self-defense after Iran had launched unsuccessful strikes against Bahrain multiple times this week.
A powerful explosion rattled homes in Riyadh on Wednesday, AFP journalists and residents said, as Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis pressed their campaign of attacks against Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis also said they intercepted two cruise missiles — the latest in weeks of strikes targeting military, civilian and oil infrastructure.
Later on Wednesday, the coalition said it had intercepted two drones launched by the Houthis in the Riyadh and southern regions, after Saudi authorities had issued and later lifted an alert for the southern Sharurah governorate.
Residents said Wednesday's explosion came without warning, with no cellphone alert issued beforehand as is usually the case during aerial threats.
"The explosion was extremely loud," said a resident in northern Riyadh. "Hearing a blast without receiving a warning is very frightening."
An AFP journalist said doors throughout her home swung open and the lights briefly went out.
The location of the explosion was not immediately clear, but residents told AFP they saw smoke near Riyadh's airport in the northeast of the city.
U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Wednesday that Iranian threats inside and outside the U.S. have "dramatically increased."
"We remain committed to detecting, deterring and combatting the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States," Clayton told members of the House Homeland Security Committee during a hearing. "These threats have dramatically increased."
He emphasized the danger posed by online radicalization, describing how foreign extremist networks can influence individuals already living inside the United States.
"That's not theoretical; it's real," Clayton said.
Deputy FBI Director Christopher Raia noted that intelligence about possible plots does not necessarily mean would-be attackers have the capability to carry out the plans.
"A lot of the reporting is largely aspirational," Raia said. "But that does not mean we do not take it seriously."
Saudi Arabia is preparing for its war against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen to last well into 2027, the Reuters news agency reported Wednesday, citing two Western officials briefed by the kingdom about its planning.
Fighting in Yemen's grueling civil war between the Houthi rebels and Yemen's Saudi-backed government had largely stopped after a ceasefire was signed in 2022, but reignited over the summer as the war launched by the U.S. and Israel against Iran sent tension across the Middle East surging.
The exchange of fire between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been more intense than the other fronts in the intertwined Middle Eastern conflicts since U.S.-Iran hostilities eased late in the summer. Thousands of people have been killed and hundreds of thousands displaced in Yemen, and Houthi rockets have killed at least 20 people in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi authorities have acknowledged Houthi targeting of key infrastructure in the kingdom, including airports and oil facilities. The kingdom now expects the campaign to last up to six more months, Reuters said, adding that Saudi officials are hoping to see advances on the ground before re-entering negotiations with the Houthis.
This week, however, has seen Yemeni government-aligned forces pull back from some key territory on the Red Sea coast as the Houthis take more ground.
The U.S. military's Central Command shared new images Wednesday of the USS Theodore Roosevelt and USS George Washington aircraft carriers sailing in tandem in the Arabian Sea.
CENTCOM included a photo compilation of the two nuclear-powered carriers in a post on X that offered no information, just a date and the vague location of the carrier in the sea, which is southeast of the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf beyond.
The U.S. military's naval presence in the Gulf of Oman, the Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean is currently greater than the force deployed during Operation Epic Fury, at the peak of U.S. and Iranian hostilities, according to an open source intelligence analysis by the independent Israeli think tank The Institute for National Security Studies.
The U.S. military confirmed Monday that there are now three aircraft carrier strike groups in the region after the recent arrival of the USS Roosevelt. It joined the USS George H.W. Bush and USS Washington, alongside a slew of associated destroyers and other vessels.
The three-carrier presence is expected to be temporary, as carrier strike groups rotate through the region.
Iran on Wednesday rejected as "completely unfounded" an assertion by authorities in North Macedonia that they had uncovered a Tehran-backed assassination plot targeting a person in Greece.

articles.title_zh: Israeli tanks roll into central Gaza in first ground operation since ceasefire began
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of displaced Palestinians fled their tents and shelters in central ‌Gaza on Wednesday as Israeli tanks advanced, in what the Israeli military said was an operation targeting Hamas infrastructure outside areas that Israel controls in ⁠the enclave.
Witnesses said some Israeli tanks rolled onto the main Salahudeen road, west of the Yellow Line that marks the boundary of the two-thirds of the Gaza Strip still under Israeli control despite ⁠a ceasefire that has ​lasted more ⁠than a year.
An Israeli airstrike near the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
The medics ⁠said separate Israeli airstrikes had killed two other people ​earlier ⁠in the day in ‌ Deir al-Balah and Gaza City.
An Israeli military spokesperson told NBC News that the military was carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of ‌the Yellow Line in central Gaza ‌and that it had struck a militant in southern Gaza earlier on Wednesday.
They later confirmed that it was the first ground operation since the U.S. brokered ceasefire came into effect in October 2025 .
Dozens of Palestinians, most of whom have been displaced multiple times since the start of the war in 2023, piled their belongings on top of bicycles, wheelchairs, motorcycles and vehicles as ​they fled the area.
Salam Aql said the military had ordered residents of the area to leave “but we wanted to stay because we ​are exhausted from being displaced so many times.”
“We are tired, I swear to God, we are tired. But as we were sitting there, gunfire started ‌coming ⁠in,” she said, adding that a boy was hit in the leg by a bullet.
“Once he was wounded, we could not stay any longer.”
Hamas said the Israeli military’s raid and forced displacement of Palestinians marked a ceasefire violation and a ​dangerous escalation.
The truce halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war, although it has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas’ disarmament.
The Israeli military spokesperson had no immediate comment on other strikes.
Residents reported hearing tank shells being fired in the area. An Israeli airstrike near the location of the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
Israel, which says Hamas has recently been regrouping and rearming, has stepped up attacks against the Islamist group. Hamas has accused Israel of attempting to derail the U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement.
Gaza health ‌authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been ​killed since the ceasefire went into effect, while ‌the Israeli military says five Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Palestinian authorities say more ⁠than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the military campaign ‌that Israel ​launched there after Hamas-led fighters killed ‌about 1,200 people in southern ​Israel in an attack on October 7, 2023.
The body overseeing US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the Gaza war on Wednesday ​accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments to end hostilities, leaving the population of Gaza in dire conditions and the ‌ceasefire in danger of collapse.
The 12-page Board of Peace report, seen by Reuters, is the body’s second to the United Nations Security Council since the US-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a sobering assessment of progress made since then.
The board, established and headed by Trump, is expected to present the report’s findings to a meeting of the council in New York at ​the end of November.
“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” ​the report said, warning that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.”
While the ceasefire has halted major ⁠fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect ​last year.
Hamas agreed in July to a Board of Peace roadmap to surrender its weapons and transfer governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority, but Israel rejected the ​roadmap, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas is dismantled.
Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza, while the report said Hamas fighters have also continued attacks on Israeli troops.
“Every day that Israel continues strikes against Hamas targets, it delays putting Hamas’ agreement to the roadmap to the test,” the report said.
“Meanwhile, Hamas militant activity continues, the commitment to cease all military activities has not ​been met in full by the parties, and the population faces another winter in tents and rubble.”
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim dismissed the report as “pure disinformation”, accusing the ​Board of Peace of providing cover to Israel to evade its commitments under the plan to end the war and to continue its aggression in Gaza.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister ‌Benjamin Netanyahu ⁠and a spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping’s family history runs deep
articles.title_zh: Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping’s family history runs deep
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — It took a trip to China for me, an American, to see U.S. President Donald Trump in person for the first time.
Trump emerged from a group of black-clad photographers and other personnel surrounding him at a welcome banquet in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting held Nov. 17 to 19.
Seated just a few spots to his left was Russian President Vladimir Putin who picked up a glass of red wine to join a toast led by Chinese President Xi Jinping .
"At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results," Xi said in Mandarin, according to a CNBC translation.
Xi was speaking broadly, but Thursday's agenda includes a bilateral meeting with Trump, and their highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Putin.
But looking at the mood in the room, it seemed that their trilateral conversation had already started Wednesday night at their long banquet table. Much of what happens at APEC, including bilateral meetings and other exchanges between leaders, takes place away from the media.
But what struck me was how little sign there was of the tension surrounding Nvidia 's CEO Jensen Huang resignation, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days.
Ahead of Trump's entrance into the banquet hall, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shared a friendly moment with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other members of the American delegation.
Last week, the U.S. officials said that Trump did not plan to raise allegations of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy during his meeting with Xi.
It was a striking contrast to just two months ago, when I saw photographs of Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk sharing a table with Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C.
And when Trump visited Beijing in May, Huang took a few minutes to speak with reporters, including me, inside the Great Hall of the People. Musk was there too, accompanied by one of his sons.
This time, neither were visible in a room that was closely watched by the world. Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen, but I did not see him Wednesday evening.
Their absence from the government-heavy banquet was striking. The world's most powerful leaders may be grappling with the implications of artificial intelligence, but they certainly didn't need the industry's biggest names at the table to do so.
China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers
Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition
Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
Over the months I've spent following APEC's "China Year," one thing has become clear: The forum has given Beijing an opportunity to host the U.S., Japan and other member economies at a time when unresolved tensions might otherwise have made such gatherings difficult.
But even in a year defined by talks of U.S.-China "strategic stability," the APEC events have exposed the rifts and the shifting dynamics in global power. Those dynamics were on display for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
Several hundred attendees, from Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, arrived early for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
After waiting in silence for at least 10 minutes, the audience welcomed Xi in a distinctly modern way: by raising their smartphones to capture the moment. The applause was rather muted.
It was much the same at the more government-heavy welcome banquet that evening. So many attendees rushed to take their own photographs of Xi and other leaders entering the room that reporters' views were largely blocked.
Following Xi's morning speech, there was a lengthy intermission before Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim took the stage.
"The entire multilateral framework needs to change," he said, praising China on its "rare" recognition of smaller countries.
During the tea break that followed, attendees quickly resumed mingling. Some even brought coffee and snacks back into the room as Putin prepared to speak.
They listened as the Russian president talked about his country's economic resilience and claimed Europe was losing ground. As attendees headed to lunch, one thing stood out: Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader had taken the stage at the opening event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon.
The most visible American presence during the morning session came from business leaders appearing in a promotional video ahead of Xi's speech.
And the absence of an American voice was perhaps even more noticeable at Wednesday evening's banquet.
Trump did not follow Xi with a toast of his own. This was the same famously outspoken president, who in a winding speech in Davos, had declared that the U.S. must get Greenland .
Yet on Wednesday night in China, Trump wasn't the one holding the microphone.

articles.title_orig: Almost nobody’s vying for an invite to Trump’s second meme coin dinner
articles.title_zh: Almost nobody’s vying for an invite to Trump’s second meme coin dinner
articles.content_orig:
Plus, high-stake negotiations are underway at the United Nations over killer robots, Palantir’s CEO is trying to rebrand his company as “progressive” and more — all in this week’s Tuesday Tech Drop.
Happy Tuesday! Here’s your Tuesday Tech Drop, some of the past week’s top stories from the intersection of politics and technology.
According to a new report from Reuters, the value of President Donald Trump ’s meme coin has cratered to record lows ahead of a cryptocurrency gala this weekend at his South Florida estate. The report also says that interest in the president’s third such gala “has collapsed.”
Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat who is primed to become chair of the House Oversight Committee in January, told MS NOW that looking at Trump’s crypto ventures — and investors who may have felt legitimately scammed — will be a priority for his committee.
A federal judge has issued a permanent injunction barring the Justice Department or Department of Homeland Security from pressuring Apple to suppress Eyes Up, an app used for documenting immigration enforcement activity.
Read more at the Indiana Capital Chronicle .
As Trump continues to voice support for Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s CEO amid a scandal involving his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, scrutiny continues to mount over the president’s financial stake in the company behind some of the world’s most-coveted computer chips . My colleague Steve Benen wrote about recent reports on the timing and frequency with which Trump has traded Nvidia stock that raise even more questions.
High-stakes negotiations are underway at the United Nations as representatives gather this week to discuss potential regulations on lethal autonomous weapons.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp, whose tech firm has been central to Trump’s racist anti-immigrant crackdown , is trying to rebrand his company as “progressive” after Democrats’ blue wave in the midterms.
Trump has invested in several of the companies that his transportation secretary wants to build a multibillion-dollar network for the Federal Aviation Administration after last week’s nationwide ground stop debacle, and I wrote about the president’s financial entanglements.
An Army major and whistleblower said Pentagon leaders shrugged off warnings about the need for adequate protection before an Iranian drone strike killed six U.S. service members. Trump responded by raging at CBS News’ “60 Minutes” for airing the claims — without disputing their merits.
Lauren Chen, a right-wing influencer who has been accused of being paid by the Russian government to peddle pro-Kremlin propaganda to American audiences, made a recent appearance at the president’s Mar-a-Lago property in Florida.
Read more at The New Republic.
After making history by winning his Senate race in Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom still has questions about how his state used inaccurate data from Experian to mark some voters as inactive ahead of this year’s midterms. Now, Mississippi’s Republican secretary of state is warring with the credit reporting company as those questions swirl.
Read more at Democracy Docket .
Ja’han Jones is an MS NOW opinion blogger. He previously wrote The ReidOut Blog.
Ask MS NOW's Mychael Schnell about the major investigations Democrats are lining up as they prepare to take control of Congress.

articles.title_orig: Americans will pay more for Thanksgiving dinners this year, Farm Bureau says
articles.title_zh: Americans will pay more for Thanksgiving dinners this year, Farm Bureau says
articles.content_orig:
For the first time since 2022, American shoppers will see an increase in the price of goods for Thanksgiving dinner. Results from the American Farm Bureau Federation's 41st annual Thanksgiving dinner cost survey indicate that the price of a Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people averages $58.63, up 6% from a year ago.
Over Four Decades of AFBF Thanksgiving Surveys
Each November, as millions of Americans prepare to gather with their family and friends to celebrate Thanksgiving, hundreds of volunteer shoppers from all 50 states and Puerto Rico participate in AFBF's annual Thanksgiving dinner cost survey. Every year since 1986, shoppers have reported prices for a standard list of items at their local grocery store for a variety of ingredients used to craft Thanksgiving favorites. Up until 2018, the survey included carrots, celery, cranberries, cubed stuffing, dinner rolls, frozen green peas, sweet potatoes, pumpkin pie mix, frozen pie crusts, whole milk, heavy whipping cream, and the ubiquitous American holiday staple: turkey. In 2018, AFBF added ham, frozen green beans and russet potatoes to better reflect the price of an all-American Thanksgiving meal.
While the overall cost of Thanksgiving dinner ticked upward in 2026, prices for several items included in the survey decreased slightly from 2025. A vegetable tray containing celery and carrots posted the largest percentage decline in this year's survey, with a 3.7% decrease compared to a year ago. In terms of absolute dollar changes, frozen pie crusts had the sharpest decrease, posting a decrease of 9 cents compared to a year ago. The survey bodes well for pumpkin pie enthusiasts, who will enjoy a lower overall cost for their beloved dessert despite an increase in the cost of pumpkin pie mix, as heavy whipping cream is also cheaper in 2026 compared to last year.
Higher Prices for Several Thanksgiving Favorites
The overall cost of a 10-person Thanksgiving dinner increased for 2026, largely fueled by increases in items key to the Turkey Day menu. The most notable increase for 2026 is the turkey itself, with the average price of a 16 pound frozen bird being $23.68, an increase of $2.38 (10%) from 2025. As discussed in a recent Farm Bureau Intel , strong demand and tight inventories have led to increased prices for turkey in 2026.
Apart from turkey, other widely featured Thanksgiving items increased in this year's survey. Grocery store prices for boneless ham, milk, dinner rolls, sweet potatoes, russet potatoes, frozen peas, frozen green beans, cranberries, and cubed stuffing (known in some regions as “dressing”) all increased in 2026.
Higher prices for these items aren't a complete surprise, as the effects of significant spikes in prices for critical inputs throughout the supply chain, like fuel for processing and transportation, have made their way to consumers. America's farmers and ranchers also face significant challenges, with record diesel costs, elevated fertilizer prices, increased labor expenses, and a bigger bill for items like rent and electricity — all of which hurt their ability to breakeven at the end of the year. However, unlike wholesalers and retailers, farmers aren’t able to pass those costs up the supply chain
Thanksgiving Dinner Prices Vary Across the Country
At an average of $61.57 for a 10-person classic Thanksgiving dinner, the Northeast has the highest cost. The Northeast's dinner basket cost is about 5% higher than the national average.  The average cost for a Thanksgiving dinner for 10 in the West and Midwest is closer to the national average, at $58.74 and $56.89, respectively. The South's average dinner cost is $54.33.
Some Shoppers May Find Great Deals
Despite the overall increase in the average cost of Thanksgiving dinner this year, some of our shoppers were able to find staggering deals on a variety of items, including turkey, which some shoppers reported finding  for as low as 69 cents per pound, nearly half the average nationwide price for a pound of turkey.  As Thanksgiving approaches, shoppers will look for deals on a variety of items to bring down the cost of their Thanksgiving dinner grocery list.
Higher Grocery Prices Do Not Mean Higher Farm Profits
Farm Bureau's 2026 Thanksgiving Dinner market basket survey indicates that Americans will pay more to feed family and friends this Thanksgiving. Nearly all items surveyed increased in price compared to 2025, with turkey, milk and cranberries posting some of the largest year-over-year percentage gains. However, higher grocery prices do not necessarily translate into better returns for America's farmers and ranchers.
Farmers and ranchers are largely price-takers, not price-makers, and receive only a small share of what consumers spend at the grocery store. USDA's Food Dollar Series estimates that less than 6 cents of every dollar spent on food goes back to the farm. Even when higher retail prices translate into increased farm revenue, rising production costs can quickly offset those gains. Elevated prices for critical inputs such as diesel, fertilizer and equipment continue to squeeze farm margins.
For example, this year's survey found that a 12-ounce bag of cranberries costs nearly 9% more than last year. That increase does not necessarily mean the Wisconsin cranberry farmer who grew them is receiving a higher price. Even if the farmer does capture some additional revenue, those earnings are needed to cover increased fertilizer, fuel and other production expenses.
As Americans gather around the Thanksgiving table, it's important to remember that higher food prices can place pressure on both consumers and the farmers who produce that food. Wherever and however you celebrate this Thanksgiving, take a moment to thank America's farmers and ranchers, who continue working through challenging economic conditions to provide the food, fuel and fiber we rely on every day.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia, Take-Two, Palo Alto, Applied Optoelectronics, TJX, and More Stocks That Explain Today’s Market
articles.title_zh: Nvidia, Take-Two, Palo Alto, Applied Optoelectronics, TJX, and More Stocks That Explain Today’s Market
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia wavered after the embattled chipmaker reported quarterly figures that beat expectations and issued strong guidance.
Take-Two Interactive also got a boost ahead of the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI", while Lowe's shares pulled back following the company posting third-quarter results.
Follow along as CNBC covers the biggest stock market moves of the day.
Companies tied to cybersecurity gained in Wednesday's trading on the heels of a warning from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency of a "critical Java vulnerability."
The federal agency warned on Tuesday that organizations should "immediately patch" a memory-corruption vulnerability that's known as "Java4Shell."
The Global X Cybersecurity ETF (BUG) was last up 6%, as was Palo Alto Networks . CrowdStrik e gained 7% and Okta advanced 9%.
Shares of TJX Companies jumped over 10% after the apparel and home fashions retailer beat on revenue for the third quarter against analyst consensus.
The company reported $1.34 per share, excluding items and $15.95 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by FactSet also anticipated $1.34 per share and $15.82 billion in revenue.
TJX adjusted its full-year earnings guidance to range between $5.17 and $5.20 per share, up from $5.15 to $5.20 a share.
The State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE) tumbled nearly 3% on Wednesday as oil prices dropped.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were last down 4.5% to about $82 a barrel, while international Brent futures dropped 2.5% to trade around $90 a barrel.
Chevron , ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips each shed around 3%.
Shares of crypto exchange Bullish surged 12% midday following the company's strong third-quarter financial update.
Bullish posted adjusted net income of $18.7 million, trouncing analyst expectations of $12.7 million, per FactSet. Adjusted revenue came in at $84.4 million, topping FactSet consensus estimates of $79.8 million.
The company also lowered its full-year outlook for adjusted operating expenses to between $220 million and $225 million, from a range from $225 million to $230 million, and said its board authorized a share repurchase program of up to $300 million.
Shares of Cal-Maine Foods are up nearly 9% after the company said Wednesday that ⁠it would cull about 1.8 million ​birds after ​avian influenza ​was detected at one of its Florida facilities , forcing the ⁠U.S. ‌egg producer to temporarily ⁠halt production at the site.
As the largest egg company in the U.S., it announced the suspension of production ‌at the facility while following U.S. Department of Agriculture ​protocols.
The company said it will cull 1.4 million laying hens and 360,000 pullets, equal to 2.7% of its flock.
Neocloud stocks CoreWeave and Iren cut earlier gains and went negative on the session as of midday trading.
CoreWeave was last down 3%, while Iren dropped 1% on the day. .
Both companies traded higher earlier in the session following Nvidia 's quarterly earnings beat and stronger outlook for revenue growth in the 2028 fiscal year.
Nvidia was also down 1% in midday trading.
Shares of mining companies tumbled in midday trading as the price of gold and silver slid to their lowest levels since September 2025.
Newmont Corp and Freeport-McMoRan slid more than 6%, while Southern Copper dropped 5%. Anglogold Ashanti fell nearly 8%.
Spot gold was last down 2.8% at $3,744.72 per ounce, while spot silver slid 4.9% to $45.09 an ounce.
Gold futures for December delivery tumbled almost 3% to $3,748.5, while silver futures slipped 4.9% to $45.04.
— Darla Mercado, Gina Francolla
Shares of Millicom International Cellular are up nearly 1% after JPMorgan upgraded the digital telecommunications and media company to overweight from neutral on Wednesday, maintaining a $105 price target, implying a 28% gain above Tuesday’s close of $82.
JPMorgan analyst Marcelo Santos sees a buying opportunity on the stock's recent weakness.
"Part of the weakness may have been due to technical factors, such as Tigo's removal from MSCI Sweden, and part due to the acquisition of Entel Peru, which we do not believe destroys value," Santos said.
The upgrade comes as Millicom expands in Latin America. The company agreed last week to buy Entel's Peru business for $1.71 billion, adding to its regional footprint.
Nvidia's post-earnings gains were short-lived, with the stock last down 0.4%. If the stock falls again, it would mark its fifth consecutive daily pullback.
Shares of the legacy news media company slid nearly 3% after Citi on Wednesday downgraded the stock to neutral from buy. Analyst Jason Bazinet said near-term trends in app downloads, active users, engagement frequency and time spend are all eroding. He lowered his price target to $76, from $85, which implies roughly 3% upside from Tuesday's close for the stock.
"These trends suggest New York Times may face lower sub growth due to lower conversion, lower retention, or higher churn," he wrote.
Raymond James upgraded Charles Schwab to strong buy from outperform, saying the stock is undervalued and poised for significant earnings growth driven by higher interest rates, strong customer growth and expanding lending businesses.
Shares were higher by more than 1% in premarket trading.
"We view Schwab as a clear beneficiary from higher-for-longer interest rates which should drive continued healthy net interest margin expansion," Raymond James analyst Patrick O'Shaughnessy said in a note Wednesday. "Beyond macro tailwinds, Schwab's account and net new asset growth rates are healthy and prove the company's value proposition with self-directed retail investors and RIAs remains strong. The company is also enjoying robust success with key growth initiatives such as pledged asset line lending."
Shares of neocloud companies bounced in extended trading on the back of Nvidia's quarterly report. The chip giant plays a key role in financing the AI buildout, and neoclouds have often used borrowed funds for their infrastructure.
Iren and CoreWeave each added 4%, while Nebius Group gained about 5.5%.
Shares of Dolby Laboratories fell about 4% in premarket trading after the manufacturer of audio technologies company shared guidance that missed Wall Street's expectations.
Dolby sees adjusted earnings in a range of $4.27 to $4.42 per share for the fiscal year ending September 2027 on revenue of $1.42 billion. The FactSet consensus sought $4.58 per share and $1.47 billion.
Revenue guidance for the current quarter also fell short of expectations.
Spot gold prices were off more than 2% on Wednesday and hit their lowest levels since September 2025 . Shares of some miners declined with the previous metal.
Newmont Corporation fell 3%, while Freeport-McMoRan declined 2.5%.
Shares of a slew of AI names across different verticals of the technology were higher following Nvidia's earnings after the bell on Tuesday.
Fellow chipmaker Marvell Technology jumped 3%, while memory giant Sandisk rose the same amount. Optical components manufacturer Coherent and onsite fuel cell company Bloom Energy were both higher by 4.5%.
Shares of retailer Target slipped by 1% despite the company reporting net sales growth of 7.1% in the third quarter. The figure is the company's best sales growth in five years .
Target also delivered a revenue beat, and earnings of $2.65 per share, though that figure includes 50 cents in tariff refund benefits, and it wasn't immediately clear if that was comparable to analysts polled by LSEG's estimate for $2.07 per share.
The company also hiked its full year earnings guidance to between $10.65 to $11.40 per share.
Lowe's declined more than 3% in premarket trading Wednesday after it reported third-quarter financial results .

articles.title_orig: Nvidia interim CEO says 'we’ve got this' as company looks to future without Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Nvidia interim CEO says 'we’ve got this' as company looks to future without Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
Humilis Investment Strategies CEO and CIO Brian Belski joins Taylor Riggs to analyze Nvidia's third-quarter earnings beat, showing a 103% year-over-year revenue surge. They also discuss the board's decision regarding Jensen Huang.
Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday's earnings call that the company is well-positioned to move forward following the abrupt resignation of co-founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang last week following the revelation of extramarital affairs.
Kress, who has served as Nvidia's CFO since 2013, delivered the AI giant's first quarterly earnings report since Huang's departure, which beat the market's expectations in terms of revenue and earnings per share.
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this," Kress said on the call.
"With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia's leadership position," she added.
NVIDIA RELEASES QUARTERLY EARNINGS, SUGGESTS FUTURE PLANS AFTER JENSEN HUANG'S RESIGNATION
Nvidia's quarterly earnings beat the market's expectations in its first report since Jensen Huang's resignation. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Investors were looking for the company to provide reassurance about its path forward as well as to post strong results over the prior three months in what was viewed as a test for the durability of the AI trade .
Nvidia's earnings beat analysts' estimates for quarterly revenue , which came in at $115.8 billion and topped the estimate of $109.1 billion reflected in data compiled by LSEG. Diluted earnings per share were $2.68, beating the estimate of $2.48.
Revenue was up 20% on a quarterly basis and 103% year over year, while earnings per share rose 10% from the prior quarter and 108% from a year ago. Nvidia's net income for the quarter was $65.3 billion, which represents a quarterly increase of 9% and a rise of 105% year over year.
Nvidia lifted its forecast for the fourth quarter of its fiscal 2027, which includes an additional week, to project $130 billion in revenue, plus or minus 3%; while Kress said the company raised its fiscal year 2028 outlook with revenue growth of 75% year over year, an increase from 70%.
JENSEN HUANG SAYS HE IS WILLING TO RETURN AS NVIDIA CEO, SAYING 'I OWN MY MISTAKES COMPLETELY'
Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. (Nvidia/Handout)
She also noted that Nvidia's cloud industry backlog grew to $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago, which underscored the "significant multiyear opportunity ahead of our partners and of Nvidia."
Earlier on Tuesday before the earnings release, Huang released a statement saying that "I own my mistakes completely" and that he would be open to returning as the company's CEO if the board of directors thought it would be "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America."
Harvey Jones, chairman of the Nvidia board of directors, shut down that speculation on the earnings call, saying that Huang voluntarily resigned and the board "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
NVIDIA ADDS BOARD OVERSIGHT OF NATIONAL SECURITY AND EXPORT COMPLIANCE
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would be willing to return as CEO after resigning last week, though the board chairman later said directors don't plan to do so. (Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images)
The chairman said that the company will consider internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent CEO. He added that while the board would like to name the permanent CEO soon, it isn't in a rush to do so and "won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person."
Jones also praised Kress, saying that "Colette has been at the center of this company's extraordinary growth for the last 13 years, instrumental in executing strategy and with a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position."

Nvidia shares were down about 2% in late morning trade on Wednesday following the release of the quarterly earnings report after the closing bell on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s board unanimously accepted former CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and does not intend to reinstate him as chief executive, board chair Harvey Jones said at the start of the company’s earnings call Tuesday night.
The announcement comes after Huang said in a statement earlier Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return as CEO, should the board allow it. Huang abruptly resigned last week amid national security concerns and reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Jones said Nvidia’s board has “every confidence” in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress to lead the company as it searches for a permanent leader.
The company sought to reassure investors and offer clarity about its future in the third-quarter earnings report Tuesday evening, with Kress, saying Nvidia’s “roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.”
“Our ambition will not change, our passion to innovate will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change,” Kress told investors, whose confidence in the company’s future has been badly shaken by the scandal , on the earnings call.
It’s the first financial picture investors are getting since the chipmaker was shaken last week by Huang’s resignation after three decades at the helm of the company he founded.
Nvidia more than doubled its quarterly revenue and profit from a year prior, and both figures beat Wall Street’s expectations.
Lies, spies and sex are just one part of the Nvidia story. The real stakes are much bigger
Nvidia’s earnings — the numbers and executives’ comments — have long been viewed as a bellwether for the larger AI industry, with Nvidia’s technology and funding at the heart of much of the boom. That’s especially true now with questions swirling about the industry’s future without Huang, its biggest cheerleader and dealmaker, at the helm.
Nvidia shares were coming off their worst week in 19 months heading into the report. The stock is down 16.7% since Huang admitted to an extramarital affair and Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, erasing $751 billion in market value. Since Nvidia shares hit their record high on October 6, they have dropped 35%, erasing roughly $2 trillion in market value.
Ahead of the report, Siebert Financial Chief Investment Officer Mark Malek wrote that it would be the “most important in the company’s history.”
Nvidia shares have dropped for four consecutive days since Huang resigned. Shares fell just 0.44% Tuesday. But shares moved higher in after-hours trading after the earnings release and analyst call, gaining roughly 5% as of 6:10 p.m. ET.
“The massive results, strong guidance and reassurance that the strategy Huang put in place remains firmly on track show that an orderly CEO transition does not necessarily have to dilute the company’s value,” Thomas Monteiro, senior analyst at Investing.com, said in emailed commentary following the release. He added that Nvidia’s growth train “can continue with or without Huang, provided the company makes the right call on leadership.”
Nvidia’s board said last week that Kress, the company’s CFO of 13 years, would serve as interim CEO as it considered internal and external candidates to permanently fill the role. Nvidia’s board also said Tuesday it had established a new national security and export control oversight committee to ensure the company is abiding by global trade regulations, and that it will strengthen its internal national security and compliance initiatives.
Some Nvidia employees, investors and other tech leaders had called on the board to reinstate Huang as CEO, pending the outcome of its investigation into his multiple reported extramarital affairs, including with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang , whom US officials suspect as a potential Chinese intelligence asset; and at least one direct subordinate at Nvidia.
Huang said Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return as CEO if the board decided that his “return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America,” in his first public comment since resigning.
Jones said during Tuesday’s call that he would not take additional questions regarding Huang’s resignation or the company’s investigation, but that the board would “communicate further when appropriate.” Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, joined Kress to take analyst questions on the call — a signal of his importance as a senior leader at the company.
Meanwhile, Huang is set to testify on Capitol Hill on December 1. He is expected to face questions about his relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s sales of chips to Singapore-based Megaspeed, which some US officials believed should have been labeled a national security risk.
Some US sources say that whether or not Alice Huang was recruited by China’s intelligence service, she posed a counterintelligence risk because Chinese national security law requires its citizens to assist in intelligence-gathering efforts if asked. Concerns have been mounting that chips Megaspeed purchased were diverted to Chinese entities, potentially skirting US export restrictions.
Huang’s exit aside, concerns about whether the AI trade is a bubble about to burst, with valuations and infrastructure spending outpacing returns, had already begun to reach a fever pitch in recent months. Gary Gensler, the former top cop on Wall Street, told CNN this week that he believes the AI bubble will likely burst and cause a recession prior to the 2028 presidential election.
Nvidia’s Tuesday report indicates that, at least for now, the company’s growth continues to outpace Wall Street’s expectations.
The company posted $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% year-on-year. Profits reached more than $65 billion, up 105% year-on-year. Kress also said demand for the company’s next-generation Vera Rubin AI computing technology is “off to an explosive start,” with the tech already in use by customers such as Google, Microsoft and Oracle.
Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains strong, with a handful of the biggest AI and cloud companies expected to shell out more than $1 trillion in capital expenditures next year alone. But in the wake of Huang’s exit, investors have been more concerned with the company’s future business.
The report also comes after a blue wave in the US midterm elections ushered in a slate of newly elected leaders, many of whom campaigned on slowing or restricting data center development, which could dent Nvidia’s business.
Analysts with research firm IDC wrote in a report last week that the firm sees “near-term AI infrastructure demand and supply as largely locked in, so the harder questions,” like long-term bets on emerging technologies and the financing system that Jensen Huang sat in the center of , “sit further out.”
Nvidia said it expects fourth-quarter revenue to come in around $130 billion, plus or minus 3% — exceeding what Wall Street analysts had predicted, according to consensus estimates from FactSet.
Kress raised the company’s growth estimates for next year even higher from its already-ambitious targets, saying Nvidia’s revenue is expected to grow by 75% in fiscal 2028, up from 70% in the last earnings call.
Significant questions also remain about the future of Nvidia’s business in China, and potentially in Asia more broadly, as US officials react to the national security concerns surrounding the company.
Shipments of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China made up less than 1% of sales in its core data center business in the previous quarter . However, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., estimated that China and Hong Kong “could comprise roughly 15% of revenues when considering potential loopholes throughout Asia.”

articles.title_orig: Hospitals Rush to Patch Java Vulnerabilities
articles.title_zh: Hospitals Rush to Patch Java Vulnerabilities
articles.content_orig:
The bug could let hackers take over systems at banks, hospitals and most Fortune 500 companies.
If the last week is any indication, the coming months and years will be a wild ride for digital infrastructure. After outages at Microsoft , the FAA , banks , Apple and... seemingly everything else, we've now learned that a bug in the programming language Java can be used to take over computer systems.
Researchers at cybersecurity startup Calif discovered the flaw with help from OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber model, which isn't yet publicly available. On some machines, feeding Java's base64 decoder a string of 64 "A" characters followed by an equals sign triggers a memory error. Usually, that leads to a crash. But when finessed in specific ways, it can be used to gain full unauthorized access to the system.
Calif showed that the bug could be used to hack into Keycloak, a widely used login system protecting organizations like CERN and NASA. Java is everywhere, powering platforms for banks, hospitals, airlines and government agencies; it's used by about 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies.
Fortunately, Calif says the bug isn't easy to weaponize, which should give defenders some breathing room. Oracle shipped a critical patch update on Tuesday without specifically mentioning this bug, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) told organizations to patch their systems immediately. Still, some systems will inevitably go unpatched, and Calif estimates that the bug could linger for five to 10 years.
Taken alone, the incident is troubling enough. Although officials' public statements haven't linked the past week's outages to AI, the events paint a picture of aging digital infrastructure unprepared for what's next. It turns out that "AAAAAAAA..." isn't only the way into unpatched computers; it's also what we'll increasingly be saying as this 21st-century arms race unfolds.

articles.title_orig: Israeli Tanks Advance Across Gaza Cease-Fire Line in Rare Incursion
articles.title_zh: Israeli Tanks Advance Across Gaza Cease-Fire Line in Rare Incursion
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of displaced Palestinians fled their tents and shelters in central ‌Gaza on Wednesday as Israeli tanks advanced, in what the Israeli military said was an operation targeting Hamas infrastructure outside areas that Israel controls in ⁠the enclave.
Witnesses said some Israeli tanks rolled onto the main Salahudeen road, west of the Yellow Line that marks the boundary of the two-thirds of the Gaza Strip still under Israeli control despite ⁠a ceasefire that has ​lasted more ⁠than a year.
An Israeli airstrike near the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
The medics ⁠said separate Israeli airstrikes had killed two other people ​earlier ⁠in the day in ‌ Deir al-Balah and Gaza City.
An Israeli military spokesperson told NBC News that the military was carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of ‌the Yellow Line in central Gaza ‌and that it had struck a militant in southern Gaza earlier on Wednesday.
They later confirmed that it was the first ground operation since the U.S. brokered ceasefire came into effect in October 2025 .
Dozens of Palestinians, most of whom have been displaced multiple times since the start of the war in 2023, piled their belongings on top of bicycles, wheelchairs, motorcycles and vehicles as ​they fled the area.
Salam Aql said the military had ordered residents of the area to leave “but we wanted to stay because we ​are exhausted from being displaced so many times.”
“We are tired, I swear to God, we are tired. But as we were sitting there, gunfire started ‌coming ⁠in,” she said, adding that a boy was hit in the leg by a bullet.
“Once he was wounded, we could not stay any longer.”
Hamas said the Israeli military’s raid and forced displacement of Palestinians marked a ceasefire violation and a ​dangerous escalation.
The truce halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war, although it has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas’ disarmament.
The Israeli military spokesperson had no immediate comment on other strikes.
Residents reported hearing tank shells being fired in the area. An Israeli airstrike near the location of the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
Israel, which says Hamas has recently been regrouping and rearming, has stepped up attacks against the Islamist group. Hamas has accused Israel of attempting to derail the U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement.
Gaza health ‌authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been ​killed since the ceasefire went into effect, while ‌the Israeli military says five Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Palestinian authorities say more ⁠than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the military campaign ‌that Israel ​launched there after Hamas-led fighters killed ‌about 1,200 people in southern ​Israel in an attack on October 7, 2023.
The body overseeing US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the Gaza war on Wednesday ​accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments to end hostilities, leaving the population of Gaza in dire conditions and the ‌ceasefire in danger of collapse.
The 12-page Board of Peace report, seen by Reuters, is the body’s second to the United Nations Security Council since the US-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a sobering assessment of progress made since then.
The board, established and headed by Trump, is expected to present the report’s findings to a meeting of the council in New York at ​the end of November.
“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” ​the report said, warning that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.”
While the ceasefire has halted major ⁠fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect ​last year.
Hamas agreed in July to a Board of Peace roadmap to surrender its weapons and transfer governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority, but Israel rejected the ​roadmap, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas is dismantled.
Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza, while the report said Hamas fighters have also continued attacks on Israeli troops.
“Every day that Israel continues strikes against Hamas targets, it delays putting Hamas’ agreement to the roadmap to the test,” the report said.
“Meanwhile, Hamas militant activity continues, the commitment to cease all military activities has not ​been met in full by the parties, and the population faces another winter in tents and rubble.”
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim dismissed the report as “pure disinformation”, accusing the ​Board of Peace of providing cover to Israel to evade its commitments under the plan to end the war and to continue its aggression in Gaza.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister ‌Benjamin Netanyahu ⁠and a spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.
